g.passage: While the cook ladled broth into two paper bowls, Clara explained the plan a second time: they would tell Clement's father that the school trip had been canceled, and the trip money would go toward his birthday surprise instead. Clement poked at a slice of pork and said nothing. When she finished, he asked how many birthdays she had planned before, and she admitted this was her first. He snorted, but he slid the chili oil across the counter to her, the way his father always did, and told her that the lie would need a better reason for the cancellation. She took out a pen and wrote his suggestion on a napkin. Steam rose against the striped awning, and a bus hissed to a stop at the corner.

g.passage: Salt-stained binoculars hung by the door of the lighthouse station where Marta wrote her novels, and I lifted them only to have something to do with my hands. I had come to deliver proofs, expecting the polite distance of a writer and her translator. Instead I watched Larissa read a paragraph aloud in Persian, pause, and wait while Marta mouthed the English sentence beneath it, as if checking a pulse. Marta's family, passing through with tea, called Larissa the helper. Yet when Larissa frowned at a word, Marta crossed out her own line rather than defend it, and later asked her, almost shyly, which of two endings she should keep. Outside, the lamp turned its slow beam over the rooftops, and a dog barked twice at the gate.

options: Larissa feels inferior to Marta and hesitates to question any part of her work.
Marta treats Larissa as a trusted collaborator whose judgment shapes the writing.

g.explanation: 가족은 라리사를 단순한 조수라고 부르지만, 방문자인 화자는 다른 모습을 본다. 라리사가 한 단어에 얼굴을 찌푸리자 마르타는 자신의 문장을 지우고, 나중에는 두 결말 중 무엇을 남길지 라리사에게 묻는다. 이 두 단서는 마르타가 라리사의 판단을 신뢰하고 작품에 반영한다는 것을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A와 C는 의존의 방향을 잘못 읽었고, D는 지문이 뒤집는 통념이다.

g.passage: Diesel and burnt coffee hung over the bus depot in Istanbul where Nikos and I had worked the night schedule for twenty-two years. We rarely talked; a nod at the start of each shift had always been enough. One evening I opened the dispatch drawer looking for a stapler and found a stack of my own letters to my mother, the ones I believed had been lost years ago, each stamped and returned. Nikos must have been keeping them safe since the depot's old mailroom closed. I said nothing. The next night he set a cup of tea at my elbow before I asked, and I left the drawer unlocked so he would know I had seen. Through the glass, a bus idled with its doors folded open, its headlights pale in the drizzle.
g.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between the narrator, Mingyu, and Nikos?
options: Mingyu feels betrayed by Nikos's secret and quietly withdraws from their friendship.
Nikos waits anxiously for Mingyu to explain the letters he found in the drawer.

Like most coworkers, they share a schedule but have little personal connection.
g.explanation: 화자는 두 사람이 거의 말하지 않고 고개 끄덕임만으로 충분했다고 말한다. 서랍 속 편지를 발견한 뒤에도 말없이, 니코스는 차를 건네고 화자는 서랍을 잠그지 않은 채 두어 알았다는 신호를 보낸다. 두 장면을 이어 보면 말없는 몸짓으로 서로를 이해하는 깊은 우정이 드러나므로 C가 정답이다. A는 감정을 잘못 추측했고, B는 설명을 기다리는 방향을 뒤집었으며, D는 지문과 어긋나는 통념이다.

g.passage: Who brings a ferry token to a wedding? Mele asked, watching Leilani turn the brass coin over her knuckles while the band tuned up. Leilani explained that her father gave one to every passenger who crossed the harbor in bad weather, a promise that the boat would come back for them. Mele had ridden that ferry for years; tonight she was only waiting for a message from the hospital where her brother lay in surgery. As the speeches began, Leilani pressed the token into Mele's palm. Mele held it through the toasts and the first dance, rubbing its worn edge whenever her phone stayed dark. When the screen finally lit, she did not read it at once. She closed her fingers around the brass first. Around them, guests clapped as the couple cut a cake shaped like a lighthouse.
g.question: In the text, the ferry token most likely represents
options: the debt that Mele owes Leilani's father for her many years of crossings.
Leilani's wish to leave the crowded wedding and return to the harbor.
the long friendship that Leilani and Mele formed while riding the ferry.
a promise of safe return that Mele clings to while she awaits the news.
g.explanation: 레일라니는 아버지가 궂은 날씨에 승객에게 배가 다시 데리러 온다는 약속으로 토큰을 주었다고 설명한다. 이후 멜레는 수술 중인 오빠의 소식을 기다리며 휴대전화가 꺼져 있을 때마다 토큰을 문지르고, 소식이 오자 먼저 토큰을 쥔다. 두 단서를 이으면 토큰은 무사 귀환에 대한 약속, 즉 기다림 속 희망을 상징하므로 D가 정답이다. A, B, C는 지문 어휘를 쓰지만 토큰의 반복된 쓰임과 연결되지 않는다.

g.passage: Ofelia found the jar on her workbench at four in the morning, its lid still tied with the red string she had used when she gave it away. Inside, the sourdough starter had been fed and was bubbling, alive. She had kept that culture going for eleven years, feeding it every night before the ovens warmed, and she had handed a portion to Ingrid after their first month together on the night shift, telling her it would need her every day. Ingrid, shaping rolls at the far table, did not look up. Later she mentioned, to no one in particular, that her lease ended in spring and she had not decided where she would go. Ofelia unscrewed the lid, smelled the sour sweetness, and set the jar on the shelf beside her own. Flour drifted in the light above the proofing racks, and outside, the first delivery van rattled over the cobbles.
g.question: In the text, the sourdough starter most likely represents
options: an ongoing commitment that Ingrid feels unable to promise she will keep.
Ofelia's resentment that Ingrid has ignored her advice about baking bread.
the bakery's eleven-year history and its constant need for new workers.
Ingrid's gratitude, shown by feeding the starter before she returned it.
g.explanation: 오펠리아는 반죽 효모를 11년 동안 매일 돌봐 왔고, 잉그리드에게 나눠 주며 매일 돌봐야 한다고 말했다. 잉그리드는 효모를 돌려준 뒤 봄에 임대가 끝나 어디로 갈지 정하지 못했다고 말한다. 두 단서를 연결하면 효모는 매일의 지속적인 헌신을 상징하며, 잉그리드는 그것을 약속할 수 없어 돌려준 것이므로 A가 정답이다. D는 효모가 살아 있다는 점을 근거로 한 그럴듯한 오답이지만 반환의 이유를 설명하지 못한다.

g.passage: Janelle was already at the train-station cafe in Port of Spain when I arrived, two cups of sorrel tea sweating on the table and the blue ribbon from Saturday's garden show lying between them. I had bought the house on the hill only in March; she had tended its hibiscus for thirty years before that. Everyone at the show knew her blooms were the best, and everyone saw her withdraw her entry an hour before judging, leaving mine to win. I had brought the ribbon to return it. She pushed it back across the table and said the garden needed to learn my name. A train pulled in as she spoke, and pigeons scattered from the platform roof. Since then I have kept the ribbon in a drawer rather than on the wall, and each time I see it I water more carefully, prune more slowly, as though the prize is still being judged. Outside my window now, the hibiscus has begun to bud along the fence.
g.question: In the text, the blue ribbon most likely represents
options: Janelle's lingering bitterness at losing the house to a newcomer.
the community's admiration for Shanice's skill as a gardener.

g.passage: Cut grass and wet chalk: that is what I remember of the field in Taipei the week after I missed the penalty in front of the whole stadium. Coach Yuxuan benched me without explanation. Each evening at dusk she handed me a flat ball from the equipment shed and a hand pump, and I knelt by the sideline pressing air into it while the others ran drills. At first I resented the task and pumped carelessly, so the ball sagged by morning. By the fourth night I was checking the valve, squeezing the seams, testing the bounce against my palm before I handed it back. Yuxuan never commented. On the last evening of the week she rolled the ball back to me and pointed at the penalty spot. The floodlights buzzed on, one bank at a time, and moths gathered in the glare.
g.question: In the text, the flat ball that the narrator, Ruoxi, inflates each evening most likely represents

Ruoxi's lasting resentment toward the teammates who watched her fail.
the team's dependence on Ruoxi to keep all of its equipment in order.

g.explanation: 화자는 페널티킥 실수 뒤 벤치에 앉게 되고, 코치는 매일 바람 빠진 공을 채우게 한다. 처음에는 대충 해서 공이 아침이면 다시 처졌지만, 나흘째에는 밸브와 솔기를 꼼꼼히 확인하게 된다. 마지막 날 코치가 그 공을 페널티 지점으로 굴려 주는 장면까지 이어 보면, 공은 실수로 비어 버린 자신감이 서서히 다시 채워지는 과정을 상징하므로 D가 정답이다. A와 B는 초반의 원망에만 기댄 오답이고, C는 상징을 문자 그대로 읽었다.

g.passage: Jeju Island had one bus stop on that stretch of the mountain road, a tin shelter where Minjun waited each afternoon after school. Eamon, who had fished with her father before her father left for Busan, sat down beside her and said, without greeting, that her aunt had heard. Minjun had told only one classmate that her father was not coming back. By the time Eamon reached the shelter, the story had already walked down the mountain without her, stopping at the market, the clinic, and finally her aunt's kitchen. Eamon offered her a tangerine and said her aunt was not angry, only hurt that she had learned it from a neighbor. Minjun peeled the fruit slowly. Mist slid over the ridge, and the bus appeared, its headlights soft in the gray.

g.passage: Your hives sound quieter this year, Amelia said, setting her bag on the bench by the gate. Sota, who had taught her chemistry thirty years earlier in Porto Alegre, only lifted the lid of the nearest box and let her look. Fewer frames held comb; the bees moved over them slowly. He told her that he had sold four colonies in the spring and would sell the rest in autumn, though he said it as if describing the weather. Amelia asked who would keep them. He answered that the bees had been humming a smaller song for some time now, and that he had been pretending not to hear it. She helped him close the lid. Neither of them mentioned his hands, which shook as he tightened the strap. Along the fence, the jasmine had opened, heavy with afternoon heat.

g.passage:
Why keep the shutters open, Emilio asks,
when no one climbs the hill for gloves anymore?
Bronislaw, who stitched beside his grandfather
for forty years, sets down his guesthouse cup
and listens to the bell for vespers.

A shop, he says, is a lamp left burning
for a traveler you have never met.
You do not light it for the road tonight.
You light it so the road remembers.

Emilio looks down at his grandfather's thimble,
worn to silver on one side,
and counts the unpaid bills again.

Below the cloister, Naples gathers its lights,
and a cat crosses the warm stones of the yard.

g.passage: Themba had driven me to the vineyard gate every harvest morning for six years, and I had never once paid attention to the route until the season I took a job picking grapes for his cousin's rivals across the valley outside Addis Ababa. He still stopped for me. He still saved the seat behind him. But he no longer hummed along to the radio, and when I mentioned the new owners' generous wages he simply nodded at the windshield. That autumn I felt as if I were pruning the same vine from both sides, trimming one friendship to feed another and unsure which branch would bear fruit. On the last day of harvest I bought two baskets of grapes, one from each estate, and left his on the dashboard. Dust rose behind the bus as it climbed toward the hills, gold in the evening light.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “pruning the same vine from both sides” most nearly suggests that the narrator, Zawadi, was
options: working harder at the harvest than she had in any earlier season.

g.passage: Our mother's radio still works. Thuy proved it the morning she arrived at the dock in Manila, turning the dial until a station crackled through the static, though we had not spoken in nine years. She had come to decide which of us would keep it. We sat on the planks with our feet above the water, and the silence between us had its own tide: it drew back when she laughed at an old song, then rushed in again whenever one of us said our mother's name. Aung, she said finally, you take it. I said she should, since she was the one who had fixed the antenna. By noon neither of us had touched it. A fishing boat slid past the pilings, and its wake slapped softly against the posts.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the silence between us had its own tide” most nearly suggests

the noise of the lake drowning out the sisters' conversation.

g.explanation: 두 자매는 9년 동안 말을 하지 않았고, 화자는 둘 사이의 침묵이 밀물과 썰물처럼 움직였다고 말한다. 언니가 옛 노래에 웃을 때 침묵이 물러났다가 어머니의 이름이 나오면 다시 밀려왔다는 설명이 이어진다. 따라서 이 표현은 추억에 따라 줄었다가 다시 생기는 거리감을 뜻하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 결정이 나지 않은 결말과 맞지 않고, B는 비유를 문자 그대로 읽었으며, D는 서로 라디오를 양보하는 모습과 어긋난다.

seed.topicSeed: a printing press room in Shanghai; an elder and a restless apprentice after a surprising success that makes things harder

g.passage: Shanghai, in the old tale, held a press room so small that only two people could turn its great wheel: Jordan, the elder printer, and Xinyi, an apprentice who could not sit still. One winter Xinyi set the type for a book of riddles without asking permission, and by spring every bookseller along the river wanted a thousand copies. Merchants crowded the doorway. Paper ran short, ink froze in its pots, and Xinyi slept beside the wheel. Jordan watched her for many nights before speaking. You planted one seed, he told her, and now it wants the whole garden. Xinyi asked whether she should have planted nothing. Jordan only handed her a second lamp and showed her how to trim its wick. Outside, snow settled on the rooftops of the sleeping town.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “now it wants the whole garden” most nearly suggests that
options: the riddle book will soon be copied by rival printers in town.
Xinyi should leave the press room to work as a gardener.
Jordan regrets having taught Xinyi to set type by herself.
a small success has grown into demands that consume everything.
g.explanation: 신이가 허락 없이 만든 수수께끼 책이 크게 성공하자 상인들이 몰려들고 종이와 잉크가 바닥나며 신이는 바퀴 옆에서 잠을 잔다. 조던은 씨앗 하나를 심었더니 이제 정원 전체를 원한다고 말하며 작은 시작이 모든 것을 요구하게 되었음을 비유한다. 이어 두 번째 등불을 건네는 행동도 더 많은 수고가 필요함을 암시하므로 D가 정답이다. B는 비유를 문자 그대로 읽었고, A와 C는 지문에 근거가 없다.
